A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UIP2P, with the same authors and underlying framework despite the renamed subtitle. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original UIP2P evaluations on IP2P and MagicBrush, qualitative editing results, loss and inference-step ablations, and a 52-participant user study.

after.justification: V2 retains original UIP2P experiments and reports additional benchmark results, a timestep ablation, and a revised 50-participant user study.

M1.justification: CEC is renamed ERC, but the IP2P architecture, SD-v1.5 initialization, four loss terms, and forward/reverse algorithm remain equivalent. Algorithm 1 already added noise to the input image in v1. V2's explanations of single-step training and attention layers do not establish a changed procedure.

E1.justification: V2 adds HQ-Edit as a training dataset and PIE-Bench and Emu Edit as evaluation benchmarks, alongside the retained datasets. These substantially broaden the training and evaluation distributions within the existing instruction-based image-editing task; relocated qualitative examples do not constitute additional coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated comparators InstructDiffusion in Table 4 and PnP and Emu Edit in Table 5, and inserts IP2P into the ablation comparison in Table 3. Existing qualitative, user-study, and full MagicBrush comparator sets remain. HQ-Edit is reported as a UIP2P training variant, while the added DiffusionCLIP discussion supplies no scored comparison.

E3.justification: The user study changes from 52 participants selecting two of six outputs for 15 instructions to 50 participants making pairwise choices for 30 instructions, with 18,000 votes and Elo-based reporting. Training batch size changes from 768 to 256 and learning rate from 5e-5 to 1e-5, retaining 11K iterations; this establishes revised reported settings, not that retained experiments were rerun. New benchmark metrics and a same-timestep control further expand the protocol.

E4.justification: V2 adds a same-versus-random forward/reverse timestep ablation in Table 3, qualitative loss-component effects in Figure 6, and attention maps across noise steps in Figure 7. It removes v1's 5/15/50-step inference comparison and accompanying reduced-DDIM-step analysis. The original numerical loss ablation and reversibility examples are retained.

E5.justification: V2 introduces sequential Elo estimation for pairwise preferences, documenting initialization at 1500 and K = 32 in Appendix C, whereas v1 reports selection percentages. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-seed estimates. V2's two user-study runs refer to different assessment criteria, not repeated statistical trials.

E6.justification: V2 adds HQ-Edit-trained results, PIE-Bench and Emu Edit scores, and timestep-control outcomes. Its revised user study reports UIP2P Elo scores of 1681/1659 and adjusted win rates of 22%/23%, replacing results collected under a different protocol. All 120 numerical entries in the full MagicBrush comparison and all 15 original loss-ablation values remain unchanged. The inference-step result panel is removed.

T1.justification: The training-loss mathematics and Algorithm 1 are equivalent apart from notation and naming. Removing the standard cross-attention formula and adding standard Elo formulas changes explanatory material, without introducing new theoretical reasoning, assumptions, or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain instruction-based editing without ground-truth edited images, reversible training using semantic and spatial alignment, and scalable training on image-caption datasets. ERC terminology and additional experimental support do not materially redefine these claims. Superior editing performance and efficient training were already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive limitations concerning spatial reasoning, counting, occlusion, text rendering, photorealism, reverse-instruction quality, and training overhead. It adds interpretations of input noising, timestep variation, and HQ-Edit's benefits and constraints, while removing the reduced-DDIM-step explanation. The new claim that random timesteps improve every metric overstates Table 3: CLIP-T falls from 0.299 to 0.296.

D1.justification: Appendix H.1 newly supplies exact prompts for reverse-instruction generation and CC3M/CC12M edit expansion, documenting an important previously unspecified part of data reproduction. V2 also specifies attention-layer selection, validation-based grid search, and Elo parameters, and changes reported hardware from 16 H100 GPUs to 8 A100 GPUs. Reproducibility remains imperfect: the new expansion prompt requests four edits while the main text still states eight.

R1.justification: V2 adds discussion or citations concerning HQ-Edit, UltraEdit, CycleGAN, attention-regularization work, and Elo-based evaluation, plus references supporting the new benchmarks and comparators. Appendix I.1 expands the comparison with DiffusionCLIP. These refine the existing positioning around avoiding supervised editing triplets and fixed-domain transformations.

P1.justification: Beyond pervasive CEC-to-ERC terminology changes, v2 rewrites substantial portions of the abstract, introduction, and method explanation, compresses the background section, and reorders quantitative evaluations. The numbered appendix subsections are reorganized into thematic sections A-J, with dataset and implementation material regrouped.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is substantially redrawn, Figure 2 gains HQ-Edit examples, and qualitative panels are rearranged and annotated with arrows and circles while retaining their underlying examples. Tables 2 and 3 are restructured, new benchmark tables and diagnostic figures are added, and the inference-step and user-study-interface figures are removed.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens support for the retained method through broader benchmark evaluation and a direct timestep control, while exact generation prompts and explicit limitations improve transparency. The net gain is limited by reporting problems: training settings change without clarifying their relationship to retained scores, the new prompt requests four edits despite the stated eight, and the timestep discussion overclaims improvement across all metrics. These prevent the revision from establishing a substantial overall quality improvement.
